newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OECD urges lower Australian inflation target.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OECD urges lower Australian inflation target.

text.p: Australia should consider aiming for lower inflation once people become accustomed to its current two to three percent target, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said.
And Canberra would probably have to redouble the attack on its fiscal deficit if it were to keep its budget in balance on average over the course of an economic cycle.

"The potential for lower inflation to yield non-negligible benefits might suggest a reassessment of the numerical inflation objective by the Reserve Bank once economic agents become better accustomed to the new low-inflation environment, which should reduce the economic cost of further disinflation," the OECD said in a report released in Canberra.
For the past few years the bank has aimed to keep underlying inflation -- which excludes large irregular factors -- at an average between two and three percent.
The OECD said that target made sense because expectations were still tied to the high inflation of the past, but this would change as acceptance of Australia as a low inflation environment grew.

The OECD also said the budget tighening announced in August was probably not enough to achieve a so-called structural balance -- one in which surpluses during economic upturns balance the deficits caused by recessions. "Further consolidation measures are likely to be required to achieve sufficiently large surpluses during the remainder of the present expansion to compensate for the inevitable deterioration in the budget position during the next economic downturn," it said.

In its August 20 budget, the Australian government announced measures that would cut A$7.2 billion from its bottom line in the fiscal year to June 1998, the first year in which the measures would be fully implemented.
The upper house of parliament, the Senate, refused to authorise measures worth A$300 million to A$400 million of that total.
Before those changes, the underlying budget deficit was projected to fall from A$10.3 billion in 1995/96 to A$5.6 billion in 1996/97 towards producing a small surplus in 1998/99.
The underlying budget deficit excludes proceeds of asset sales and similar transactions.
Underlying inflation was 2.4 percent for the year to the September quarter.
